Purpose

This R Markdown file documents and reproduces the manuscript analysis for estimating waking sedentary time in NHANES 2011-2014 wrist accelerometer data. The project combines posture predictions from the CHAP wrist model with sleep/nonwear information from SWaN to estimate each participant’s usual daily waking sedentary time.

The main goal is to produce survey-weighted, nationally representative estimates of waking sedentary time after excluding sleep/nonwear periods. The analysis calibrates a sleep/nonwear percentage cutoff against NHANES self-reported sleep duration, applies the selected cutoff at the primary analysis epoch, summarizes sedentary time to the participant level, and estimates overall and subgroup means using the NHANES survey design.

This file is also a reproducibility driver. It reads the analysis-ready accelerometer datasets from the wristsed data package, derives the analytic sample, recalibrates the sleep cutoff for the 1-hour SWaN primary analysis, generates manuscript tables and figures, and writes final outputs to outputs/final_analysis/ and figures/final_analysis/.

Packages

Analysis Configuration

The primary render uses the 1-hour SWaN epoch dataset. Sleep/nonwear removal is applied at the epoch level before participant-day sedentary totals are calculated. For figures that display hourly patterns, records are aggregated to hour only after the sleep/nonwear rule has been applied.

The primary analytic unit is the NHANES participant. Epoch-level accelerometer records are used to construct participant-day and participant-level sedentary time summaries, but survey-weighted estimation is performed at the participant level to avoid giving participants with more observed records or more valid days disproportionate influence.

Data Access

Reusable Functions

Self-Reported Sleep Benchmark

NHANES self-reported sleep duration is used as an external benchmark for selecting the accelerometer sleep/nonwear cutoff. The benchmark is estimated with the same combined 2011-2014 survey design used for the primary participant analysis.

Primary 1-Hour Cutoff And Participant Data

The final sleep/nonwear cutoff is selected from a fine-resolution objective curve. For each candidate cutoff, the analysis compares survey-weighted accelerometer-derived sleep/nonwear duration with the survey-weighted NHANES self-reported sleep benchmark. The selected cutoff is the value that minimizes the absolute difference between those two sleep-duration estimates. This fine-resolution selected cutoff, not the coarse sensitivity-grid cutoff, is used for the primary waking sedentary-time analysis.

The fine-resolution objective curve selected a 1-hour SWaN sleep/nonwear cutoff of 90.84%. At this cutoff, the survey-weighted accelerometer-derived sleep/nonwear estimate was 6.91 hours/day, and the absolute difference from the survey-weighted self-reported sleep benchmark was 0.043 hours/day.

Main Estimates

Survey-weighted estimates are computed at the participant level. Each participant contributes one usual daily waking sedentary-time estimate, one waking-time estimate, and one sleep/nonwear-time estimate to the survey design.

Justification for Combining Survey Cycles

To assess whether the two NHANES cycles could be pooled, we compared survey-weighted estimates of mean sedentary time between 2011-2012 and 2013-2014. The mean sedentary time was 11.46 hours/day (SE = 0.06) in 2011-2012 and 11.25 hours/day (SE = 0.07) in 2013-2014. The survey-weighted regression estimate of the difference was -0.21 hours/day (p = 0.0251). This difference is small relative to the overall mean, so the two cycles were combined for subsequent analyses using recalibrated 4-year examination weights.

NHANES Analytic Approach

The primary estimand in this manuscript is the population mean of each participant’s usual daily waking sedentary time. The analysis therefore treats the NHANES sample person, not the hour, as the survey-weighted analytic unit. This matches NHANES guidance: sample weights are assigned to sample persons and account for unequal probability of selection, nonresponse, and post-stratification to U.S. population control totals.

The repeated accelerometer records were still used fully to derive the participant-level exposure. For each candidate sleep cutoff, SWaN sleep/nonwear percentages determined whether an epoch was treated as waking time, CHAP sitting probabilities contributed fractional sedentary hours using the epoch duration, daily totals were computed, and valid days were averaged within participant. The person-level mean is therefore a summary of all available epoch- and daily-level information for that participant.

What is intentionally removed before the main survey estimation is the repeated record structure itself, because leaving epochs or days as separate weighted records would give participants with more observed records or valid days more influence than participants with fewer records. That would change the estimand from a population mean across people to a record-weighted mean across observed person-epochs or person-days.

Notes: Direct states do not apply a sleep/nonwear cutoff. For SWaN, direct states use the underlying SWaN wake, sleep, and non-wear classifications combined with CHAP waking-sedentary time. For NHANES, direct states use the official NHANES 1-minute sleep-state classifications combined with the same CHAP posture summaries. Epoch rows first aggregate sleep/nonwear states to the listed epoch length, then classify each whole epoch as waking when its sleep/nonwear percentage is below the calibrated cutoff; epochs at or above the cutoff are counted as sleep/non-wear.

Cutoff Sensitivity Grid

This step does not select the final sleep/nonwear cutoff. It evaluates a coarse grid of candidate cutoffs in 5-percentage-point increments to summarize how survey-weighted sleep/nonwear duration and waking sedentary time change across plausible decision rules. The final cutoff used in the primary analysis is the fine-resolution value selected above.

Demographic Missingness

Demographic, anthropometric, and survey-design variables are taken from the participant-level analysis datasets and reduced to one record per participant before survey estimation. Age is grouped as <18, 18-34, 35-44, 45-64, and >=65 years. Race/ethnicity is retained using the NHANES-coded categories available in the analysis data. BMI is grouped as under/normal weight (BMI < 25), overweight (25 <= BMI < 30), and obesity (BMI >= 30). Participants with missing subgroup information are not recoded into another category; missing values are excluded only from the relevant subgroup/domain estimate.

These variables describe population heterogeneity in waking sedentary time, not repeated epoch-level covariates. Subgroup estimates for age, gender, race/ethnicity, and BMI are calculated from the participant-level survey design object using domain analyses. This preserves the NHANES design information for standard error estimation while estimating the mean for the population domain of interest.

Overview of Sedentary-Time Estimation

The analysis proceeded in the following steps:

  1. Start with wrist accelerometer data. We used NHANES 2011-2012 and 2013-2014 wrist accelerometer files.

  2. Prepare the files for prediction models. The raw files were organized by participant and day and converted into the formats needed by the posture and sleep/wear models upstream of this report.

  3. Identify sitting in 10-second epochs. The CHAP/DeepPostures model classified each 10-second epoch as sitting or not sitting.

  4. Identify sleep and nonwear. SWaN classified accelerometer records as wake wear, sleep, or nonwear; these predictions were summarized to the analysis epochs used in this report.

  5. Summarize predictions for analysis. Epoch-level predictions were converted to epoch-level percentages for the primary analysis.

  6. Choose the sleep/nonwear cutoff. Candidate cutoffs were evaluated by comparing survey-weighted accelerometer-derived sleep/nonwear duration with NHANES self-reported sleep duration.

  7. Keep only waking epochs for sedentary-time estimation. Epochs below the selected sleep/nonwear cutoff were treated as waking epochs. Epochs at or above the cutoff were removed from waking sedentary-time estimation.

  8. Calculate sedentary hours for each day. For each participant-day, sedentary percentages were multiplied by epoch duration and added across waking epochs.

  9. Average days within each participant. Daily waking sedentary-time values were averaged across each participant’s valid wear days.

  10. Use the NHANES survey design. Each participant’s usual daily waking sedentary time was analyzed using NHANES examination weights, masked variance strata, and masked primary sampling units.

  11. Estimate national and subgroup values. Survey-weighted means and confidence intervals were estimated for the full population and for subgroups defined by age, gender, race/ethnicity, and BMI category.

Comparison of sedentary time estimates across studies by measurement method, datasets, and population.
Paper Dataset & Population Method Estimate & Notes
This study NHANES 2011-2014, wrist-worn 80 Hz accelerometer data; 14,608 participants, aged 3+ years. CHAP wrist model combined with SWaN. Sedentary time: 11.3 hours/day; 66.4% of non-sleep time. Mean waking time was 17.1 hours/day after excluding sleep.
Matthews et al. (2008) NHANES 2003-2004; hip-worn ActiGraph data; 6,329 participants, aged 6+ years. Intensity threshold of <100 counts/min. Sedentary time: 7.7 hours/day; 54.9% of monitored time. Mean monitor wear time was 13.9 hours/day.
Yang et al. (2019) NHANES 2001-2016; 51,896 children and adolescents. Self-reported total sitting time from questionnaire. Sedentary time: 6.4 hours/day in adults; 8.2 hours/day in adolescents. Sitting time increased in both groups from 2001 onward.
Ussery et al. (2018) NHANES 2015-2016; 5,923 U.S. adults aged 18+ years. Self-reported sitting time on a typical day. ~6.4 hours/day. Excludes sleeping time; 25.7% of adults reported sitting for more than 8 hours per day.
